transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-09
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Recording: fireflies export
Attendees: Liam Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jonas Rhee (Redwood SE), Ravi Kumar (Quantifly Head of Platform), Laura Green (Quantifly ML Infra), Marcus Lee (CTO), Diego (Quantifly SRE)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be noisy): Quick dive on kernel choices, TRT-LLM wins single-stream latency but vLLM gives more stable batching under eviction; persistent KV helps tail lat but increases memory pressure; CUDA graphs give 30-40% perf but can blow up with dynamic shapes.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Liam: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, then we'll jump into the bench numbers and the kernel routing stuff.
[00:00:06] Ravi: Hey Liam, thanks, we're excited. Got Laura and Diego here, and Marcus might drop in late.
[00:00:12] Liam: Awesome. Priya, you wanna kick off with the topo and what we profiled?
[00:00:18] Priya: Yeah sure. So we focused on three axes: kernel selection inside the runtime, behavior when CUDA graphs are enabled, and the impact of persistent KV cache across concurrent chat sessions. I ran a small smoke first, then extended to 8xA100 on your requested seq length distribution.
[00:00:34] Laura: Quick Q, sequence distribution is 8-256 tokens, 70% short requests, is that what you used?
[00:00:40] Priya: Correct, the mixed distribution you sent, roughly 70/25/5 for short/medium/long.
[00:00:46] Jonas: Also tested int8 quantized variant with TRT-LLM plugin and a dynamic batching run with vLLM's dispatcher.
[00:00:53] Diego: And did you do persistent KV? That's our main interest, we want fast context switching between sessions.
[00:00:58] Priya: Yes, we did persistent KV in two modes: per-model persistent cache (keeps KV on GPU across calls) and ephemeral KV where cache is rebuilt per request.
[00:01:06] Ravi: Great. Start with headline numbers please.
[00:01:09] Priya: Sure. On raw 95th latency for single-stream short requests, TRT-LLM with CUDA graphs and int8 gave ~18ms, vLLM without CUDA graphs on same hardware was ~28ms. But under concurrent sessions with batching and persistent KV, vLLM's eviction behavior was more graceful; TRT-LLM saw out-of-memory trials when we pinned persistent KV plus large batch windows.
[00:01:34] Laura: Wait, OOMs even with 8xA100? Can you clarify the pattern where it happens?
[00:01:38] Priya: It's when you have persistent KV pinned on a partition and then burst to many simultaneous long contexts—C-U-D-A graphs also lock shapes and that makes us hold more temporaries during replay which exacerbates memory. We saw that when a 512-token long session started while 50 concurrent short chats were still holding KVs. It was a worst-case squeeze but real for large multi-tenant pools.
[00:01:58] Marcus: Is that a kernel bug or a capacity planning mismatch?
[00:02:02] Jonas: It's a combination. TRT-LLM aggressively fuses kernels for the common attention patterns, which is great for latency, but the fused kernels allocate certain scratch buffers under CUDA graph capture. If the runtime doesn't evict early or rebalance KV placement, you hit peak memory. vLLM chooses more granular kernels and can stream some ops off GPU, so it doesn't spike as badly but pays cost in per-token throughput.
[00:02:27] Ravi: We care about 95th tail under multi-tenant loads first, throughput second. So maybe vLLM looks better?
[00:02:33] Priya: For tail consistency yes, but there are tuning levers. With TRT-LLM we tried two mitigations: autoshrink cache (evict LRU KVs after threshold) and split-graph strategy where we break CUDA graphs at block boundaries to avoid holding temporaries across dynamic shapes. That helped; 95th improved from ~120ms in the OOM case to ~50-60ms. Still not as graceful as vLLM which stayed ~45-55ms without those interventions.
[00:02:58] Laura: Split-graph strategy sounds hairy. Does it lose the CUDA graph perf boost?
[00:03:02] Priya: Some of it, yes. Split-graph loses a bit of the end-to-end graph scheduling benefit, we measured a 10-15% drop relative to full capture but it avoids massive tails. Overall it's a trade: full-graph + fused kernels = best steady-state latency; split-graph + eviction policies = better tail resilience.
[00:03:19] Diego: How about quantization? int8 seemed attractive cost-wise. Any quality regressions?
[00:03:24] Jonas: We ran a 200-prompt eval set you provided. INT8 via TRT-LLM had minimal semantic drift on our sample, roughly 0.6% BLEU-ish equivalent diff in the small set. But long context hallucination patterns diverged slightly in 3 prompts—probably numerical noise. vLLM quantized paths are more conservative; you can get int8 but often with per-layer calibration which increases runtime complexity.
[00:03:45] Marcus: So for your recommended production config for us with 95th SLOs and multi-tenant, what do you suggest?
[00:03:51] Priya: For Quantifly I'd recommend a hybrid policy: use TRT-LLM for dedicated low-latency routes (e.g., customer-facing single-stream agents), with CUDA graphs enabled and careful split-graph fallbacks for dynamic shapes; use vLLM for multi-tenant chat pools where persistent KV and tail stability matter. Also enable quantization on the dedicated routes where quality loss is tolerable and keep fp16 for the multi-tenant pool.
[00:04:11] Laura: Will that add a lot of ops complexity to our infra? Running two runtimes is more to manage.
[00:04:15] Liam: Redwood's smart routing can abstract that — we can configure route-level policies and automatic fallback to the other runtime if your primary hits capacity or OOM. Console will show token-level cost breakdowns.
[00:04:26] Ravi: About KV eviction policies — what are the knobs? LRU? size-based? time-based?
[00:04:30] Priya: We expose LRU, size (MB) thresholds, and a lease-based TTL for pinned sessions. There's also an adaptive eviction policy we tested: it monitors tail latency and increases eviction aggressiveness when percentiles drift. That adaptive mode gave us the best balance in the mixed workload.
[00:04:45] Diego: Does adaptive require graph recapture every time? That seems expensive.
[00:04:49] Jonas: Good point. If eviction changes memory layout significantly you may need to recapture some CUDA graphs. That's why split-graph helps — fewer captures. We also have a lazy recapture path that only replays smaller subgraphs; it reduces wall-time cost but isn't free.
[00:05:02] Laura: Any stability differences you saw between Triton/try-ton-based infra and Redwood's runtime?
[00:05:07] Priya: We did a side test with Triton + TensorRT (not TRT-LLM plugin) and saw more fragmentation in buffer allocations under mixed workloads. Redwood's runtime does more active kernel selection and defers some temporaries which helped. But Triton had a simpler behavior model that sometimes made capacity planning easier. So it's again a trade.
[00:05:26] Marcus: On the security/VPC front, can we run this hybrid routing in our VPC private deployment? KMS keys must stay in our HSM.
[00:05:34] Liam: Yes, Redwood Private supports local KMS/HSM integrations and the control plane can be in your VPC. We'll ship our VPC deployment checklist and an architecture doc. SEs will help validate KMS flows.
[00:05:43] Ravi: Excellent. Back to batching: what's your guidance for dynamic batch windows vs fixed batch size? We want low latency for short chats but still high throughput.
[00:05:51] Priya: Dynamic windows tuned to latency percentiles are best: small immediate dispatch for short requests, and a tiny holdback (e.g., 5-10ms) to let a few more requests aggregate. For long sequences you batch per-token to avoid head-of-line blocking. We measured a 20-30% cost improvement with those heuristics vs naive fixed batching with minimal latency penalty on 95th if tuned right.
[00:06:12] Laura: Did you observe any bad interactions between dynamic batching and KV persistence? Like if you batch different sessions with pinned KVs, does that increase memory churn?
[00:06:20] Priya: Yes it can. If different sessions with large KVs get coalesced in a batch, you end up with combined memory spikes. Our runtime has per-batch KV planning that can refuse to coalesce incompatible sessions or will trigger pre-eviction. That's part of the adaptive policy.
[00:06:33] Diego: Can Redwood surface per-route cost/latency so product owners can pick low-cost vs low-latency?
[00:06:36] Liam: Absolutely. Console has token-level cost breakdowns and per-route dashboards with 50/95/99 percentiles and model-specific costs.
[00:06:44] Ravi: Ok good. A few noisy transcriber moments here — we might have missed some numbers. Could you put the bench spreadsheet in the Slack channel?
[00:06:50] Priya: Yep i'll upload the full spreadsheet with run configs: A) TRT-LLM full-graph int8, B) TRT-LLM split-graph persistent KV, C) vLLM dynamic batching fp16 + persistent KV. It includes tail percentiles and memory maps.
[00:07:00] Jonas: Note that the memory maps contain some internal kernel names, they might be mis-typed by the recorder as 'try-ton kernel' or similar.
[00:07:06] Laura: Haha noted.
[00:07:08] Marcus: One last question: how reproducible are these numbers on our on-prem inventory (we have a mix of L40s and A100s)?
[00:07:15] Priya: L40s trend toward slightly higher FP16 throughput but worse int8 fusion support currently; A100s are better for int8 fused kernels. We'll produce a hardware matrix in the bench doc. For on-prem, driver/CUDA versions and MIG or MPS partitioning matter a lot. We'll list exact driver combos we used.
[00:07:33] Diego: Anything else from Redwood side?
[00:07:36] Liam: We'll send the security docs, bench spreadsheet, and an initial rollout plan for the hybrid routing. Also propose a POC timeline: 2 weeks to run the bench on your infra, then a 4-week pilot with a small subset of production traffic.
[00:07:49] Ravi: Sounds good. We'll sync internally on the POC scope and share hardware access.
[00:07:53] Priya: Great, I'll get the initial runs started this week.
[00:07:57] Liam: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with assigned action items and schedule a check-in next week.
[00:08:02] Marcus: Thanks all.

(End of recording — transcript contains typical auto-transcription errors, e.g., try-ton for Triton, K-V cash for KV cache, etc.)
